claims.text: N6. Every walk of length k from n_i to n_j (i = j allowed) contains a path from n_i to n_j of length at most k; the case i = j is covered because the walk of length 0 is a path. Proved by strong induction on k by deleting the part between two equal vertices.

support.quote: Assume that a is not a path. Then, there exists a walk from u to v whose length is smaller than k.
Assume that there is a walk from u to v of length k for some k ∈ N. Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.

claims.text: N6. A path in a graph with N vertices has length at most N - 1, because a path of length k lists k + 1 pairwise distinct vertices.

support.quote: However, any path from u to v must have length ≤ n − 1, where n is the number of vertices of G (since a path of length k has k + 1 distinct vertices, but G has only n vertices to spare).

claims.text: N7. For N >= 2 and S = A + A^2 + ... + A^(N-1), the graph is connected exactly when S_ij > 0 for all i different from j. Proof: S_ij is the number of walks of length 1 to N-1 from n_i to n_j (walk counting, premise from m1, C19); a path gives a walk of length between 1 and N-1 (M2-2, i different from j); a walk gives a path (M2-1). For N = 1 the condition is vacuous and the graph is connected.

support.quote: Then the entry in the (i, j)-position of the matrix Ak is the number of walks of length k from vi to vj in G.
Then, there is a path from u to v of length ≤ k.
Then, A_G is connected if and only if b_ij ≠ 0, when i ≠ j.

claims.derivation: modules/m2.md, section 3, Theorem 2.2; script scripts/m2_connectivity_test.py checks it on three graphs by brute force

claims.text: N6/N7. A path has pairwise distinct vertices, hence pairwise distinct edges, so it is a walk with no repeated edge in the textbook's sense (Definition 1.2.12); every such walk is a walk, which contains a path (M2-1). So 'a path exists between any two vertices' and the textbook's Definition 2.1.1 (stated with its Definition 1.2.12 word 'path') describe the same graphs.

claims.text: N8. Board graph (matrix rows 0 1 0 / 1 0 1 / 0 1 0, N = 3): A^2 has rows 1 0 1 / 0 2 0 / 1 0 1, S = A + A^2 has rows 1 1 1 / 1 2 1 / 1 1 1, every off-diagonal entry is 1, so the test says connected. (A^2)_11 = 1 counts the walk n1 n2 n1, (A^2)_13 = 1 counts n1 n2 n3, (A^2)_22 = 2 counts n2 n1 n2 and n2 n3 n2, (A^2)_12 = 0.
claims.derivation: scripts/m2_connectivity_test.py, output scripts/m2_connectivity_test.out, section BOARD GRAPH; the matrix is the board's, the reading of the grid is in brief.md section 5

claims.text: N8. Disconnected graph on n1, n2, n3 with the single edge n1n2: A has rows 0 1 0 / 1 0 0 / 0 0 0, A^2 has rows 1 0 0 / 0 1 0 / 0 0 0, S = A + A^2 has rows 1 1 0 / 1 1 0 / 0 0 0; S_13 = S_23 = 0, so the test says not connected, which is right because n3 has no neighbour.

support.locator: Notes 1 and 2 on the adjacency matrix, printed p. 3
support.quote: The adjacency matrix is symmetric (i.e. equal to its transpose) if the graph is undirected. The adjacency matrix has zeros on its main diagonal (unless the graph has loops).

claims.derivation: scripts/m2_connectivity_test.py, output scripts/m2_connectivity_test.out, section DISCONNECTED GRAPH

claims.text: N9. Entries of S count walks, not paths: in the path graph n1 n2 n3 n4, S_12 = 3, counting the walks n1 n2 (length 1), n1 n2 n1 n2 and n1 n2 n3 n2 (length 3), of which only n1 n2 is a path. On the board graph S_22 = 2 counts two walks while the only path from n2 to n2 is the walk of length 0.

support.locator: text after the definitions of walk and path, p. 1

claims.text: N9. A single power is not a test: on the board graph A^(N-1) = A^2 has (A^2)_12 = 0 although n1n2 is an edge, because walks from n1 to n2 have odd length.

claims.text: N9. A search that starts at one vertex and marks the vertices it reaches finds all vertices connected to it in time O(E) because each edge is examined at most twice; the source states this for depth-first search, not breadth-first search, and says nothing about the test above. So the statement that the matrix test is not the cheapest way is an interpretation resting on this one premise and on the fact that the test forms N - 2 matrix products.

support.quote: Running time. O(E) since each edge examined at most twice.

claims.text: O1 (optional). (I + A)^(N-1) is the sum over k = 0..N-1 of C(N-1, k) A^k because I and A commute; every coefficient is at least 1, so an off-diagonal entry is positive exactly when the same entry of S is positive, and every diagonal entry is at least 1. Hence (I + A)^(N-1) has no zero entry exactly when the test holds. Board graph: rows 2 2 1 / 2 3 2 / 1 2 2; disconnected graph: rows 2 2 0 / 2 2 0 / 0 0 1.

support.quote: Then G is connected if and only if all the entries of (In + A)n−1 are positive.
